title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to scale expert guidance for novice educators in real time, especially in K-12 tutoring settings where high-quality instructional support is costly and difficult to provide at scale. The authors argue that conventional professional development is too expensive, too static, and often misaligned with the immediate needs of tutors working with students during live instruction.

To address this, they introduce Tutor CoPilot, a human-AI tutoring support system that generates expert-like pedagogical suggestions during live tutoring sessions. The system is integrated into a virtual tutoring platform used by tutors to support math instruction, and it draws on conversation context, lesson topic, and selected instructional strategies to produce guidance. Tutors can also edit, regenerate, or switch strategies, making the workflow interactive rather than fully automated.

The study was a randomized controlled trial with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students from Title I schools in a large southern U.S. district, delivered through an in-school virtual tutoring program in mathematics for grades 3-8. Results show that access to Tutor CoPilot improved student mastery on exit tickets by 4 percentage points overall, with larger gains for lower-rated or less-experienced tutors. Analyses of tutoring language suggest that treatment tutors used more high-quality strategies such as prompting student reasoning and asking guiding questions, while tutors reported the system was helpful but sometimes produced guidance that was not well aligned to grade level.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered randomized controlled trial with a sizable sample and clear causal identification, which supports strong credibility. There are some concerns about generalizability, attrition/compliance, and reliance on proximal outcomes rather than longer-term standardized achievement, so it falls short of blue.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced a modest but meaningful effect on a priority population: a 4 percentage point increase in math exit-ticket mastery, with larger gains for lower-rated tutors. The effect is practical and scalable, but the absence of larger standardized-test gains keeps it in the modest-impact range.

interventions.use_case: human-AI live tutoring support that generates real-time, expert-like pedagogical suggestions for tutors during K-12 math sessions, including hints, guiding questions, worked examples, and strategy selection
real-time instructional guidance/feedback to tutors on how to respond to student misconceptions and improve tutoring moves during live sessions

finding.finding_summary: In a preregistered randomized controlled trial with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students, students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets in mathematics than control students (62% to 66%, p<0.01). Conditional on attempting the exit ticket, treatment students were also 3 percentage points more likely to pass (p<0.01).
finding.measure: Math exit ticket pass rate (attempted and unconditional pass outcomes)

finding.finding_summary: Effects were larger for less effective tutors. Students of lower-rated tutors in the treatment group were 9 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets (56% to 65%) and students of lower-experience tutors were 7 percentage points more likely to pass (61% to 68%) relative to control. This suggests Tutor CoPilot narrowed performance gaps by helping weaker tutors achieve outcomes comparable to stronger peers.
finding.measure: Math exit ticket pass rate by tutor quality rating and tutoring experience

finding.finding_summary: Student survey outcomes did not show statistically significant differences between treatment and control. Measures of whether the tutor cared about understanding, cared about how well the student did in math, and student confidence items were mixed in sign but all non-significant.
finding.measure: Student post-session survey responses on tutor care, perceived support, and confidence in learning math

finding.finding_summary: Tutor CoPilot changed tutor discourse toward higher-quality pedagogical strategies. Using NLP classifiers over 550,000+ messages, treatment tutors were more likely to prompt students to explain and ask guiding questions, and less likely to give away answers or solution strategies; some of these shifts were reported at about 2 standard deviations on the z-scored log-odds scale.
finding.measure: Classifier-based counts of high- and low-quality pedagogical strategies in tutor chat

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed and used as a low-cost support tool, with estimated annual cost of about $20 per tutor based on observed usage. The paper argues this is far cheaper than traditional educator professional development and can scale real-time expertise without requiring extensive off-platform training time.
finding.measure: Estimated annual cost per tutor; usage-based cost analysis
